questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the components of the Panchayati Raj institutions in India at the village level?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Panchayat Samiti**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Panchayati Raj system in India is a three-tier structure consisting of the Gram Panchayat at the village level, the Panchayat Samiti at the block level, and the Zila Parishad at the district level.
 
• **The Panchayat Samiti does not operate at the village level**. It functions at the block level, acting as an intermediary body between the Gram Panchayat and the Zila Parishad.
 
• The components of the Panchayati Raj system at the village level include the Gram Sabha, Gram Panchayat, and Nyaya Panchayat.
 
• The Gram Sabha is the general assembly of all the registered voters in a village, while the Gram Panchayat is the executive body responsible for governance and development activities.
 
• The Nyaya Panchayat, where established, handles minor disputes and judicial matters at the village level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gram Sabha:**

 
 
• The Gram Sabha is the foundational body of the Panchayati Raj system, consisting of all the registered voters in a village.
 
• It plays a key role in decision-making, approving budgets, and monitoring the functioning of the Gram Panchayat.
 
 
 
• **Gram Panchayat:**
 
 
• The Gram Panchayat is the executive body of the village-level Panchayati Raj system.
 
• It is responsible for implementing development programs, maintaining public infrastructure, and ensuring welfare schemes reach the beneficiaries.
 
 
 
• **Nyaya Panchayat:**
 
 
• Nyaya Panchayats are quasi-judicial bodies established at the village level in some states to handle minor civil and criminal disputes.
 
• They aim to provide accessible and speedy justice to rural citizens without the need for formal legal proceedings.
 
 
 
• **Panchayat Samiti:**
 
 
• The Panchayat Samiti operates at the block level, coordinating and supervising the activities of the Gram Panchayats under its jurisdiction.
 
• It is responsible for planning and implementing development programs at the block level.
 
 
 
• **Zila Parishad:**
 
 
• The Zila Parishad is the apex body of the Panchayati Raj system, functioning at the district level.
 
• It coordinates development activities and provides administrative support to the Panchayat Samitis and Gram Panchayats.

questions.question: Which of the following is the primary basis for allocating seats in the Rajya Sabha among various States and Union Territories in India?

options.text: Population of each state or union territory

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Population of each state or union territory**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rajya Sabha**, the upper house of the Indian Parliament, allocates seats to states and union territories based on their **population**.
 
• The allocation is done in accordance with the provisions of **Article 80 of the Indian Constitution**, which determines the seat distribution.
 
• States with higher populations are allocated more seats, ensuring proportional representation.
 
• The population data used for this purpose is derived from the **1971 Census**, as per the **42nd Amendment of the Constitution**.
 
• As of now, the Rajya Sabha consists of **245 members**, with most representatives elected by the legislative assemblies of states and union territories.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 80 of the Indian Constitution**:

 
 
• Specifies the composition of the Rajya Sabha, including representation from states, union territories, and nominated members.
 
• States are represented by members elected by their legislative assemblies using the **single transferable vote system**.
 
 
 
• **Allocation of Seats**:
 
 
• Each state is allocated seats in proportion to its population, ensuring equitable representation.
 
• Union territories such as Delhi and Puducherry are also represented, but with fewer seats.
 
 
 
• **42nd Constitutional Amendment**:
 
 
• Freezes the use of population data for seat allocation at the **1971 Census** level, to maintain uniformity.
 
 
 
• **Role of Rajya Sabha**:
 
 
• Acts as a federal chamber to represent the interests of states and union territories in the Parliament.
 
• Ensures that the voice of smaller states is not overshadowed in legislative processes.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Small Causes Courts is correct?

options.text: They can hear appeals from Nyaya Panchayats.
They deal exclusively with criminal cases of a minor nature.
They exist in all states under a uniform nomenclature.
Their decisions are final but subject to High Court’s revision.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Their decisions are final but subject to High Court's revision.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Small Causes Courts are established to deal with civil cases of a minor financial value, ensuring quick and cost-effective justice.
 
• The decisions of Small Causes Courts are final; however, they can be revised by the High Court under its supervisory jurisdiction.
 
• These courts do not deal with criminal cases; their jurisdiction is limited to specific minor civil disputes like property disputes or money recovery cases.
 
• Small Causes Courts are governed by the provisions of the **Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887**, in states where they exist.
 
• They do not operate under uniform nomenclature across all states; their presence and structure vary depending on state-specific laws.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887:** This Act governs the establishment and functioning of Small Causes Courts, outlining their jurisdiction and procedures.
 
• **Jurisdiction:** These courts typically handle civil cases involving amounts up to a specified financial limit (varies by state) and exclude cases like marriage disputes, testamentary matters, etc.
 
• **High Court Supervision:** While their decisions are final, High Courts can revise decisions if there is a procedural irregularity or legal error.
 
• **Appeals:** Appeals from Small Causes Courts are not generally allowed unless specified under the law, emphasizing their role in quick dispute resolution.
 
• **Presence of Small Causes Courts:** They are more common in urban areas where minor civil disputes are frequent, ensuring faster resolution of such matters.

questions.question: What is the term duration for representatives in municipalities in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**5 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In India, representatives elected to municipalities serve a term of **5 years** as per the provisions of the **74th Constitutional Amendment Act**.
 
• Municipal elections are held at regular intervals to ensure democratic governance at the urban local level.
 
• During their tenure, municipal representatives oversee urban development projects, sanitation, water supply, and other civic amenities.
 
• If the municipality is dissolved before completing its 5-year term, elections must be conducted within **6 months** to reconstitute it.
 
• The **State Election Commission** is responsible for conducting municipal elections in each state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992):**

 
 
• This act provided the constitutional framework for urban local governance in India, including municipalities.
 
• It categorized municipalities into three types: Nagar Panchayats, Municipal Councils, and Municipal Corporations based on population and area.
 
• The act mandates the creation of Ward Committees in urban areas with a population of 3 lakh or more.
 
 
 
• **State Election Commission:**
 
 
• Established under Article 243K of the Constitution to oversee elections to municipalities and panchayats.
 
• Each state has its own Election Commission responsible for ensuring free and fair local elections.
 
 
 
• **Municipal Governance Functions:**
 
 
• Municipalities are responsible for urban planning, regulation of land use, water supply, sanitation, and public health.
 
• They play a crucial role in maintaining public infrastructure like roads, street lighting, and parks.
 
 
 
• **Urban Local Bodies Financing:**
 
 
• Municipalities receive funds from property taxes, grants from the state and central governments, and user charges for services.
 
• They also raise revenue through issuing municipal bonds in some cases.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about the Permanent Lok Adalat under Section 22-B of The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987?

options.text: The award of the Permanent Lok Adalat is not binding on the parties.
The Permanent Lok Adalat can handle cases up to a certain monetary limit (currently ₹1 crore).
The Permanent Lok Adalat can only act as a conciliator and cannot decide disputes.
The Permanent Lok Adalat has jurisdiction over disputes related to criminal offences.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Permanent Lok Adalat can handle cases up to a certain monetary limit (currently ₹1 crore)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Permanent Lok Adalat (PLA) is established under **Section 22-B of The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.
 
• The PLA has jurisdiction over disputes related to **public utility services** like transport, postal, telecommunication, electricity, etc.
 
• The monetary limit for cases handled by the Permanent Lok Adalat is **₹1 crore**, as per the latest regulations.
 
• The PLA has the power to decide disputes if the parties fail to reach a settlement through conciliation.
 
• The award passed by the Permanent Lok Adalat is **final and binding** on the parties and is treated as a decree of a civil court.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Conciliation Mechanism:** The PLA primarily focuses on conciliating disputes and tries to bring parties to a mutually acceptable solution without litigation.
 
• **Public Utility Services:** These include essential services like water supply, electricity, transport, postal services, telecommunication, and other utilities as defined under the Act.
 
• **Binding Nature of Awards:** Awards made by Permanent Lok Adalats are treated as final and binding, making them cost-effective and time-saving alternatives to litigation.
 
• **Difference from Lok Adalats:** Unlike Lok Adalats, Permanent Lok Adalats have the authority to decide disputes even if conciliation efforts fail.
 
• **Exclusion of Criminal Offences:** The Permanent Lok Adalat does not have jurisdiction over disputes related to criminal offences or cases outside the scope of public utility services.

questions.question: Which is NOT an advantage of a Lok Adalat?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Right to appeal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Lok Adalat decisions are **final and binding** on both parties, ensuring disputes do not escalate further.
 
• There is **no provision for an appeal** against the decision made in a Lok Adalat to maintain efficiency and avoid prolonged litigation.
 
• Lok Adalats are known for **speedy resolution** of disputes, avoiding lengthy court procedures.
 
• They provide **cost-effective justice** by eliminating court fees and reducing financial burden on litigants.
 
• Lok Adalats aim to resolve disputes through **mutual consent and compromise**, promoting harmony between parties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **What is Lok Adalat?**

 
 
• Lok Adalat, meaning "People's Court," is a statutory mechanism under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
 
• It resolves disputes through **conciliation and compromise**, without a formal judicial trial.
 
• It is aimed at reducing the burden on regular courts and providing quick justice.
 
 
 
• **Legal Basis:**
 
 
• The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 empowers Lok Adalats to resolve civil, matrimonial, and compoundable criminal cases.
 
• Its primary focus is on disputes where parties are willing to resolve issues amicably.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Lok Adalat:**
 
 
• Lok Adalats help reduce the backlog of cases in courts.
 
• They provide free and speedy justice, ensuring accessibility for economically weaker sections.
 
• There is no strict adherence to procedural laws, making the process informal and efficient.
 
 
 
• **Limitations:**
 
 
• Decisions are binding and final, meaning no further appeal can be made.
 
• Lok Adalats can only handle cases where both parties agree to a settlement; contested cases are referred back to regular courts.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India states about a directive to states for the settlement of international disputes by arbitration?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 51d**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 51 of the Indian Constitution falls under the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) and promotes international peace and security.
 
• Clause (d) of Article 51 specifically encouraging the settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
 
• It emphasizes the peaceful resolution of international disputes through arbitration.
 
• This article reflects India’s commitment to maintaining amicable and cooperative international relations.
 
• It aligns with the principles of the United Nations Charter, promoting global harmony and dispute resolution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• The DPSPs are guidelines for the State to establish a just and equitable society, enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution.
 
• They are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by courts but hold moral and political significance.
 
 
 
• **Arbitration in International Law:**
 
 
• Arbitration is a method of resolving disputes outside courts, where a neutral third party (arbitrator) gives a binding decision.
 
• It is commonly used in international disputes to avoid prolonged litigation and maintain diplomatic relationships.
 
 
 
• **United Nations Charter:**
 
 
• The UN Charter, established in 1945, is the foundational treaty of the United Nations and promotes peace, security, and cooperation among nations.
 
• India, being a founding member of the UN, aligns its constitutional provisions like Article 51 with the principles of the Charter.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Article 51 reflects the ideals of the Indian freedom struggle, emphasizing peaceful coexistence and respect for international law.
 
• It was inspired by global efforts post-World War II to prevent conflicts through diplomatic and legal means.

questions.question: Which Directive Principle of State Policy is NOT added by the 42ⁿd Constitutional Amendment Act of the Constitution of India?

options.text: Protection of the environment, forests and wildlife
Promotion of democratic control of co-operative societies
Promotion of equal justice and to provide free legal aid to the poor
Secure participation of workers in the management of industries

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Promotion of democratic control of co-operative societies**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 added several Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) to Part IV of the Constitution.
 
• Key additions by the 42nd Amendment included:

 - Protection of the environment, forests, and wildlife (Article 48A).

 - Secure participation of workers in the management of industries (Article 43A).

 - Promotion of equal justice and provision of free legal aid to the poor (Article 39A).
 
• Promotion of democratic control of co-operative societies is not part of the additions made by the 42nd Amendment Act.
 
• Promotion of co-operative societies was later addressed by the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, which introduced Article 43B.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act:**

 
 
• Known as the "Mini Constitution" due to its extensive changes.
 
• Added new DPSPs to emphasize environmental protection, equal justice, and workers' participation in industries.
 
• Strengthened the socialist and welfare objectives of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs):**
 
 
• Part IV of the Indian Constitution outlines DPSPs, which are non-justiciable rights aimed at guiding the state to create a welfare society.
 
• They are inspired by the Irish Constitution and reflect Gandhian, socialist, and liberal ideas.
 
 
 
• **97th Constitutional Amendment Act:**
 
 
• Introduced Article 43B, promoting voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, and democratic control of co-operative societies.
 
• Added Part IXB, dealing with co-operative societies, to ensure their democratic and efficient functioning.
 
 
 
• **Key Articles related to DPSPs:**
 
 
• **Article 39A:** Equal justice and free legal aid.
 
• **Article 43A:** Workers' participation in industrial management.
 
• **Article 48A:** Protection of the environment, forests, and wildlife.

questions.question: Which case is associated with the Supreme Court striking down the 99th Constitutional Amendment (NJAC)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association Case (2015)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association Case (2015)** resulted in the Supreme Court striking down the 99th Constitutional Amendment, which sought to establish the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC).
 
• The judgment reaffirmed the **primacy of the judiciary in the appointment of judges** to higher courts through the Collegium system.
 
• The Supreme Court ruled that the NJAC was **unconstitutional**, as it infringed upon the independence of the judiciary—a basic feature of the Constitution.
 
• The case emphasized the importance of maintaining the separation of powers between the judiciary, executive, and legislature.
 
• The judgment was delivered by a Constitution Bench comprising **five judges**, who held that the NJAC violated the principle of judicial independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **99th Constitutional Amendment:** This amendment aimed to replace the Collegium system with the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) for appointing judges to higher judiciary.
 
• **Collegium System:** The Collegium system is a mechanism by which the Chief Justice of India and senior judges recommend appointments and transfers of judges in higher judiciary.
 
• **Judicial Independence:** It is a fundamental feature of the Indian Constitution that ensures the judiciary is free from interference by the executive and legislature.
 
• **Basic Structure Doctrine:** Introduced in the Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973), this doctrine prevents Parliament from altering the fundamental features of the Constitution, including judicial independence.
 
• **National Judicial Appointments Commission Act:** Enacted in 2014, this Act was struck down along with the 99th Constitutional Amendment in the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association Case.

questions.question: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution does the High Court exercise its original jurisdiction by issuing writs?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 226**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 226 of the Indian Constitution empowers High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and other legal rights.
 
• The writ jurisdiction includes issuing writs like habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto.
 
• Unlike Article 32 (Supreme Court), Article 226 covers not only fundamental rights but also other rights established by law.
 
• The High Court's writ jurisdiction extends to persons, authorities, and governments within its territorial limits.
 
• Article 226 serves as a vital mechanism for judicial review and upholding the rule of law in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Writs in India:**

 
 
• **Habeas Corpus:** Protects against unlawful detention.
 
• **Mandamus:** Directs authorities to fulfill their duties.
 
• **Prohibition:** Prevents lower courts from exceeding their jurisdiction.
 
• **Certiorari:** Transfers cases to higher courts for review.
 
• **Quo Warranto:** Challenges the legality of a person's public office holding.
 
 
 
• **Article 32 vs Article 226:**
 
 
• Article 32 is limited to enforcement of fundamental rights.
 
• Article 226 includes fundamental rights and other legal rights.
 
 
 
• **Territorial Jurisdiction:** High Courts can exercise writ jurisdiction over entities within their geographical boundaries.
 
• **Judicial Review:** Article 226 plays a crucial role in ensuring the accountability of public authorities and safeguarding individual rights.
 
• **Importance:** Article 226 is considered broader in scope than Article 32 and is essential for maintaining constitutional governance.

questions.question:
Which of the following is/are correct with respect to the World Trade Organization (WTO)?

1. WTO agreements cover trade in goods as well as services to facilitate international

 trade. 2. It aims to remove tariff as well as non-tariff barriers and provide greater market

 access to all member countries.

3. India has kept its commitments towards liberalisation of trade, made in the WTO, by removing quantitative restrictions on imports and reducing tariff rates.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2: 1, 2 and 3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **World Trade Organization (WTO)** governs global trade rules among its member nations to ensure fair and equitable trade practices.
 
• WTO agreements encompass trade in goods, services, and intellectual property rights, fostering international trade and economic integration.
 
• It aims to eliminate both **tariff and non-tariff barriers**, enhancing market access for member countries.
 
• India has fulfilled its WTO commitments by removing **quantitative restrictions** on imports and progressively reducing tariff rates on various goods.
 
• The WTO currently has 164 member countries (as of 2023), and decisions are made through consensus to ensure fair representation of all members.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Non-Tariff Barriers:** These include quotas, licensing requirements, and technical standards that impede international trade even without imposing tariffs.
 
• **Quantitative Restrictions:** These refer to explicit limits on the quantity or value of goods that can be imported or exported, which India removed as part of its WTO obligations.
 
• **General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS):** A key WTO agreement aimed at promoting trade in services such as banking, telecommunications, and tourism.
 
• **Dispute Settlement Mechanism:** The WTO provides a platform for resolving trade disputes among member countries, ensuring compliance with agreed trade rules.
 
• **Special and Differential Treatment (S&DT):** Developing countries, including India, are granted flexibility in implementing WTO agreements and additional time to meet commitments.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India prohibits the State from discriminating against the use of wells, tanks and places of public entertainment?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Article 15**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 15** of the **Constitution of India** prohibits the state from discriminating against any citizen on grounds of **religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.**
 
• The second clause of **Article 15(2)** specifically prohibits discrimination in accessing **shops, public restaurants, hotels, and places of public entertainment**, as well as the use of **wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly by State funds.**
 
• This article aims to ensure **equality** and abolish all forms of social discrimination that restrict access to public amenities.
 
• It is part of the **Fundamental Rights** under the Constitution, emphasizing equality and safeguarding the rights of marginalized groups.
 
• The provision ensures the promotion of an **inclusive society**, fostering harmony and equal opportunity for all citizens of India.
 
• It reflects the core values of **justice, equality, and fraternity** enshrined in the **Preamble of the Constitution.**
 
• This article plays a crucial role in reducing the practices of untouchability and other forms of discrimination in Indian society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 18**__

 __
 
• **Article 18** deals with the **abolition of titles**, except for academic and military distinctions.
 
• It prohibits the state from conferring titles and prevents Indian citizens from accepting titles from a foreign state.
 
• This article ensures the principle of equality and eliminates any form of aristocracy.
 
 
 
• **Article 17**__
 __
 
• **Article 17** abolishes **untouchability** and forbids its practice in any form.
 
• It is a significant provision aimed at eradicating caste-based discrimination in Indian society.
 
• Any act of untouchability is an **offense** punishable under law.
 
 
 
• **Article 16**__
 
 
• **Article 16** guarantees **equality of opportunity** in matters of public employment.
 
• It prohibits discrimination in public employment on the grounds of **religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence.**
 
• The article, however, allows for **reservation policies** for socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes, and Scheduled Tribes.

questions.question: In October 2024, the Mediation Act, 2023 came into force. What is a key feature introduced by this legislation?

options.text: It replaces arbitration and conciliation with mediation as the sole dispute resolution method.
It mandates that all mediation proceedings must be conducted only by retired judges.
It abolishes the role of mediators in public sector disputes.
It makes mediation compulsory for all civil and commercial disputes before court proceedings.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It makes mediation compulsory for all civil and commercial disputes before court proceedings**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Mediation Act, 2023 introduces **mandatory pre-litigation mediation** for civil and commercial disputes, aiming to reduce the burden on courts.
 
• This legislation promotes a **time-bound dispute resolution mechanism**, ensuring faster settlements through mediation.
 
• The Act establishes a **Mediation Council of India** to regulate the conduct of mediators and mediation institutions.
 
• It provides legal recognition to **mediated settlement agreements**, making them enforceable as court decrees.
 
• The Act encourages participation of trained mediators, ensuring professional and impartial facilitation in dispute resolution processes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mediation:**

 
 
• Mediation is a voluntary and collaborative process where disputing parties work with a neutral third party (mediator) to resolve their issues.
 
• It differs from arbitration as it does not involve binding decisions made by a third party.
 
 
 
• **Mediation Council of India:**
 
 
• Established under the Mediation Act, 2023, the council oversees the accreditation of mediators and mediation service providers.
 
• It aims to standardize mediation practices across India.
 
 
 
• **Mediated Settlement Agreements:**
 
 
• These agreements, reached through mediation, carry legal enforceability under the Act.
 
• They are treated as final and binding, similar to court decrees.
 
 
 
• **Pre-litigation Mediation:**
 
 
• This process requires disputing parties to attempt mediation before approaching the court.
 
• It helps in reducing litigation costs and court congestion.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India prevents any child below the age of 14 years from being employed in the factory, mine or hazardous occupation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 24**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 24** of the Constitution of India prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 years in factories, mines, or any hazardous occupations.
 
• This provision is part of the fundamental rights under the **Right against Exploitation** outlined in the Constitution.
 
• The article aims to protect children from exploitation and hazardous working conditions that can harm their physical and mental health.
 
• It aligns with the government's commitment to ensuring the welfare and development of children by preventing child labor in unsafe environments.
 
• India has ratified international conventions such as the **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child** and the **ILO Convention No. 182** to combat child labor.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Child Labor Prohibition and Regulation Act, 1986:**

 
 
• This act regulates the working conditions for children and prohibits their employment in hazardous occupations.
 
• It defines hazardous occupations and processes where child labor is strictly prohibited.
 
 
 
• **The Right to Education Act, 2009:**
 
 
• This act ensures free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years, thereby indirectly combating child labor.
 
• Education is seen as a key tool to prevent children from being exploited in the workforce.
 
 
 
• **National Child Labor Project (NCLP):**
 
 
• Under this initiative, children withdrawn from hazardous work are enrolled in special schools to provide education, nutrition, and vocational training.
 
• The program aims to rehabilitate child laborers and integrate them into the mainstream education system.
 
 
 
• **International Initiatives:**
 
 
• India is a signatory to the **ILO Minimum Age Convention (No. 138)**, which sets the minimum age for employment.
 
• The **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)** also emphasize the elimination of child labor under Goal 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth).

questions.question: What type of majority is required to pass laws under Articles 2 and 3, as per Article 4(2) in Indian parliament?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Simple majority**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Articles 2 and 3** of the Indian Constitution deal with the admission or establishment of new states and the alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of existing states.
 
• As per **Article 4(2)**, laws made under Articles 2 and 3 require only a **simple majority** in Parliament, not a special or two-thirds majority.
 
• A **simple majority** means that the majority of members present and voting in each house of Parliament is sufficient to pass the law.
 
• Unlike constitutional amendments (which often require special or two-thirds majorities), these laws are considered ordinary legislation.
 
• This provision ensures flexibility in reorganizing states to address administrative and political needs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Simple Majority:**

 
 
• A simple majority is achieved when more than 50% of the members present and voting support a motion.
 
• This is the most commonly used voting method for passing ordinary bills in Parliament.
 
• It excludes abstentions and absent members from the total count.
 
 
 
• **Special Majority:**
 
 
• A special majority requires a higher threshold, such as two-thirds of the members present and voting, or in some cases, two-thirds of the total membership of the house.
 
• It is typically required for constitutional amendment bills under Article 368.
 
 
 
• **State Reorganization:**
 
 
• State reorganization involves altering the boundaries, names, or areas of states to address linguistic, cultural, or administrative concerns.
 
• Examples include the formation of Telangana in 2014 and the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Articles 2 and 3:**
 
 
• Article 2 allows Parliament to admit new states or establish new states on terms it deems fit.
 
• Article 3 enables the reorganization of states through changes in boundaries, areas, and names.
 
 
 
• **Article 4(2):**
 
 
• It specifies that laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not considered constitutional amendments.
 
• Thus, they can be enacted through a simple majority, unlike constitutional amendment bills.

• The President of India has the authority to dissolve the Lok Sabha before its normal term expires, but this action must be taken **on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.**
 
• This power is derived from **Article 85(2)(b)** of the Indian Constitution, which allows the President to dissolve the Lok Sab

questions.question: What must State legislators do under Article 188 of the Constitution of India before taking their seats for the first time in state assembly?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Take oath or affirmation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Under Article 188 of the Indian Constitution, every member of the State Legislature is required to **take an oath or make an affirmation** before taking their seat in the State Assembly or Council.
 
• The oath or affirmation is administered by the **Governor of the state or a person appointed by the Governor**.
 
• The purpose of the oath is to ensure that legislators uphold the **integrity of the Constitution and discharge their duties faithfully.**
 
• A member cannot participate in the proceedings of the legislature or vote until they have taken the **prescribed oath or affirmation.**
 
• The format of the oath or affirmation is provided in the **Third Schedule** of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 188:** This article falls under Part VI of the Constitution, which deals with the states and specifies the rules for oaths or affirmations of State Legislators.
 
• **Third Schedule:** It contains the prescribed forms of oaths or affirmations for various constitutional posts, including State Legislators.
 
• **Governor's Role:** The Governor, as the constitutional head of the state, is responsible for administering the oath or appointing someone to do so.
 
• **Consequences of Not Taking Oath:** A legislator who does not take the oath cannot participate in legislative proceedings, vote, or receive any privileges associated with their role.
 
• **Similar Provision for Parliament:** Article 99 of the Constitution provides a similar requirement for members of the Parliament to take an oath or affirmation before assuming their duties.

questions.question: Who among the following appoints the Chairman of the National Human Rights Commission of India?

options.text: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The President of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Chairman of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) of India is appointed by the **President of India**.
 
• The appointment is made based on the recommendations of a **high-level committee** constituted for this purpose.
 
• The high-level committee includes the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Leaders of the Opposition in both Houses, and the Union Home Minister.
 
• As per the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, the Chairman of NHRC is a retired Chief Justice of India or a judge of the Supreme Court.
 
• The NHRC is an independent statutory body, and the President's appointment ensures its functional autonomy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Human Rights Commission (NHRC):**

 
 
• The NHRC was established on **October 12, 1993**, under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
 
• It is tasked with the protection and promotion of human rights in India, including the right to life, equality, and dignity.
 
• It investigates complaints of human rights violations and makes recommendations to the government for remedial action.
 
 
 
• **Composition of NHRC:**
 
 
• It consists of a Chairman, four full-time members, and four deemed members.
 
• The full-time members include one former Supreme Court judge, one former Chief Justice of a High Court, and two experts in human rights.
 
• The deemed members are the Chairpersons of the National Commissions for SCs, STs, Minorities, and Women.
 
 
 
• **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993:**
 
 
• This Act provides the legal framework for the establishment of the NHRC and State Human Rights Commissions.
 
• It defines "human rights" as rights relating to life, liberty, equality, and dignity guaranteed under the Constitution or international covenants.
 
 
 
• **Tenure of the NHRC Chairman:**
 
 
• The Chairman holds office for a term of 3 years or until the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier.
 
• He/she is eligible for reappointment.

questions.question: What power does the President of India hold regarding the Contingency Fund of India?

options.text: The President approves the annual disbursement of the fund.
The President controls the fund to advance money for unforeseen expenses.
The President can only advise on the use of the fund.
The President delegates the control of the fund to the Finance Commission.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The President controls the fund to advance money for unforeseen expenses**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Contingency Fund of India is established under Article 267 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The President of India has the authority to control the Contingency Fund and advance money for unforeseen or urgent expenditure.
 
• The fund is operated by the Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Finance, under the President's authority.
 
• This fund is utilized for expenditures that cannot wait for parliamentary approval due to the urgent nature of the situation.
 
• Once the expenditure is incurred, it is subsequently regularized by obtaining parliamentary approval through the presentation of a Supplementary Budget.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Contingency Fund:** It is a fund set aside to meet emergencies or unforeseen expenses that require immediate action.
 
• **Amount Allocated:** The Contingency Fund of India currently has a corpus of Rs. 500 crore, which can be increased if necessary.
 
• **Regularization Process:** Expenditure from the fund must be approved by Parliament retrospectively to ensure accountability.
 
• **State-Level Contingency Funds:** Similar funds exist at the state level, where the Governor exercises control over the fund.
 
• **Ministry of Finance's Role:** The fund is managed by the Ministry of Finance, ensuring efficient and transparent utilization of resources.

questions.question: Which Act empowered Her Majesty to issue Letters Patent for setting up High Courts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indian High Courts Act, 1861**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian High Courts Act, 1861, empowered the British Crown to establish High Courts in India by issuing Letters Patent.
 
• The Act replaced the Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats in the presidency towns with High Courts, combining their powers and jurisdiction.
 
• The first High Courts under this Act were established in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras in 1862.
 
• These High Courts were granted both civil and criminal jurisdiction, marking a significant reform in India’s judicial system.
 
• The Act served as a foundational step in the creation of a unified legal system in British India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Letters Patent:** A legal instrument issued by the British Crown, granting authority to establish High Courts in India.
 
• **Presidency Towns:** Major administrative centers under British rule, including Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
 
• **Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats:** These were the highest courts in the presidency towns before the establishment of High Courts. The Indian High Courts Act, 1861, consolidated their functions.
 
• **Judicial Reforms:** The Act was part of broader legal reforms aimed at streamlining the judicial system in British India, ensuring uniformity and efficiency.
 
• **Significance:** The High Courts established under this Act continue to function as the highest courts at the state level in India after independence, playing a pivotal role in the Indian judiciary.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a category of judicial review, as classified by Justice Syed Shah Mohammed Quadri?

options.text: Judicial review of administrative action of the Union and State and authorities under the state
Judicial review of judicial appointments to the Supreme Court and High Courts
Judicial review of legislation of the Parliament and State Legislatures and subordinate legislations

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Judicial review of judicial appointments to the Supreme Court and High Courts**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Judicial review refers to the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative acts, executive orders, and other governmental actions.
 
• Justice Syed Shah Mohammed Quadri classified judicial review into three categories: **review of legislative action, executive/administrative action, and constitutional amendments**.
 
• The judicial review of judicial appointments to the Supreme Court and High Courts is **not considered a separate category of judicial review** under this classification.
 
• The appointments of judges to the higher judiciary are primarily governed by the "Collegium System" and Articles 124 and 217 of the Indian Constitution, and their review is not a distinct judicial review category.
 
• Judicial review primarily focuses on safeguarding the Constitution and ensuring that no law or action violates fundamental rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Judicial Review of Legislative Action:** It involves examining laws passed by Parliament or State Legislatures to ensure their compliance with the Constitution.
 
• **Judicial Review of Administrative Action:** It ensures that administrative decisions by the executive or other authorities are not arbitrary, capricious, or unconstitutional.
 
• **Judicial Review of Constitutional Amendments:** The judiciary reviews amendments to ensure they do not violate the "basic structure" of the Constitution, as established in the landmark Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).
 
• **Collegium System:** It is a mechanism for appointing judges to the higher judiciary in India, involving the Chief Justice of India and senior judges of the Supreme Court.
 
• **Basic Structure Doctrine:** This doctrine ensures that certain fundamental principles of the Constitution cannot be altered, even by constitutional amendments.

questions.question: According to the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which body functions as the foundation of the Panchayati Raj system, ensuring broad-based community participation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gram Sabha**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Gram Sabha is the cornerstone of the Panchayati Raj system as established by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
 
• It consists of all the registered voters of a village or a group of villages within the jurisdiction of a Panchayat.
 
• Gram Sabha ensures direct participation of the community in decision-making, empowering local governance.
 
• Key functions of the Gram Sabha include approving village development plans, monitoring the implementation of projects, and ensuring transparency in Panchayat operations.
 
• It serves as the ultimate authority in the Panchayati Raj system, promoting democratic decentralization at the grassroots level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992:**

 
 
• This Act provided constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions, ensuring decentralized governance.
 
• It mandates the establishment of Gram Sabha in each village or group of villages.
 
• Three-tier structure of Panchayati Raj: Gram Panchayat (village level), Panchayat Samiti (block level), and Zila Parishad (district level).
 
 
 
• **Nyaya Panchayat:**
 
 
• Nyaya Panchayats are judicial bodies functioning to resolve minor disputes at the village level.
 
• They are distinct from Gram Panchayats and focus solely on justice delivery.
 
 
 
• **Zila Parishad:**
 
 
• Zila Parishad operates at the district level, coordinating activities between block-level Panchayats.
 
• It formulates development plans and oversees their implementation across the district.
 
 
 
• **Gram Panchayat:**
 
 
• Gram Panchayats are executive bodies at the village level responsible for implementing developmental schemes.
 
• They work under the supervision of the Gram Sabha.

questions.question: With reference to the 40th Amendment Act, 1976, which category of maritime zones came under the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Territorial waters and EEZ**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 40th Amendment Act, 1976, brought **Territorial waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), and other maritime zones** under the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament.
 
• This amendment added **Entry 25 to the Union List** in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India, empowering Parliament to legislate on these areas.
 
• The aim was to align India's constitutional framework with **international maritime laws**, specifically the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).
 
• The amendment reinforced India's **sovereign rights** over resources in these maritime zones, including fisheries, oil, and natural gas exploration.
 
• This was a crucial step in establishing a clear legal framework for India's maritime boundaries and jurisdiction over its waters.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Territorial Waters:**

 
 
• Territorial waters extend up to **12 nautical miles** from the baseline of a coastal state.
 
• The state has **sovereignty** over these waters, including the airspace above and the seabed below.
 
 
 
• **Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ):**
 
 
• The EEZ extends up to **200 nautical miles** from the baseline.
 
• In this zone, the coastal state has **special rights** regarding the exploration and use of marine resources, including energy production from water and wind.
 
 
 
• **Continental Shelf:**
 
 
• The continental shelf is the seabed and subsoil that extends beyond the territorial waters, up to **200 nautical miles** or more, depending on geological criteria.
 
• The coastal state has sovereign rights for exploring and exploiting natural resources in this area.
 
 
 
• **United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS):**
 
 
• UNCLOS, also known as the **Law of the Sea Treaty**, was adopted in **1982**.
 
• It defines maritime zones such as territorial waters, EEZ, and continental shelf and establishes the rights and responsibilities of nations regarding the use of oceans.
 
 
 
• **India's Maritime Claims:**
 
 
• India has a coastline of approximately **11,084** **km** and an EEZ of **2.37 million square kilometers**.
 
• The legislative jurisdiction over maritime zones enables India to safeguard its strategic, economic, and environmental interests.

questions.question: Which of the following sentences passed by a Sessions Judge requires mandatory confirmation by the High Court?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Capital punishment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Capital punishment, also known as the death sentence, when passed by a Sessions Judge, requires **mandatory confirmation by the High Court** as per Section 366(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
 
• The Sessions Judge cannot execute the death sentence unless it is confirmed by the High Court, ensuring a higher level of judicial scrutiny.
 
• This procedural safeguard is implemented to ensure that the decision to impose capital punishment undergoes rigorous evaluation to prevent miscarriage of justice.
 
• Capital punishment is considered the most severe form of punishment and is reserved for rarest of rare cases such as heinous crimes.
 
• The High Court reviews the legality, validity, and appropriateness of the death sentence passed by the Sessions Court before issuing confirmation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC):**

 
 
• The CrPC is the main legislation governing criminal procedures in India.
 
• Under Section 366(1), it mandates High Court confirmation for death sentences imposed by Sessions Judges.
 
 
 
• **Rare Cases Doctrine:**
 
 
• Capital punishment in India is awarded only in the "rarest of rare cases" as established by the Supreme Court in the landmark case of *Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab* (1980).
 
• This doctrine ensures that death sentences are given only for exceptionally heinous crimes with sufficient justification.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Safeguards:**
 
 
• Mandatory High Court confirmation acts as a safeguard against errors or biases in lower court decisions.
 
• It ensures that the decision undergoes detailed scrutiny by experienced judges.
 
 
 
• **Execution Process:**
 
 
• Once the High Court confirms the death sentence, the convict has the right to appeal to the Supreme Court.
 
• Additionally, the convict can file a mercy petition to the President of India under Article 72 of the Constitution or to the Governor under Article 161.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in Part IV of the Indian Constitution?

options.text: Promotion of international peace and security
Promotion of Hindi language as a medium of expression
Provision for free and compulsory education for children
Organisation of agricultural and animal husbandry

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Promotion of Hindi language as a medium of expression**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Part IV of the Indian Constitution deals with the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), which provides guidelines for the establishment of a just society.
 
• The promotion of Hindi language as a medium of expression is not explicitly mentioned in Part IV of the Constitution.
 
• Article 51 of Part IV mentions the promotion of international peace and security as one of the Directive Principles.
 
• Other provisions under Part IV include the organisation of agricultural and animal husbandry (Article 48) and the provision for free and compulsory education for children (Article 45).
 
• The Directive Principles aim to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life, ensuring equality and welfare for all.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Part IV - Directive Principles of State Policy:**

 
 
• Directive Principles are non-justiciable guidelines for governance provided to the State.
 
• These principles are inspired by the Irish Constitution and aim to achieve socio-economic justice.
 
• They are categorized into economic and social, Gandhian, and international principles.
 
 
 
• **Article 51 (Promotion of International Peace):**
 
 
• The State shall promote international peace and security.
 
• It aims to maintain just and honorable relations between nations and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
 
 
 
• **Article 45 (Education for Children):**
 
 
• The Constitution mandates free and compulsory education for children until they reach the age of 14 years.
 
• This was later reinforced by the Right to Education Act, 2009.
 
 
 
• **Article 48 (Agriculture and Animal Husbandry):**
 
 
• The State shall endeavor to organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines.
 
• It also aims to preserve and improve breeds and prohibit the slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch and draught cattle.
 
 
 
• **Promotion of Hindi Language:**
 
 
• Provisions related to the promotion of Hindi language are covered under Part XVII (Articles 343-351) of the Constitution.
 
• It emphasizes the development of Hindi as the official language and its enrichment by assimilating elements from other Indian languages.

The correct answer is __**State List**__.

questions.question: In its advisory capacity, the Union Cabinet’s advice to the President of India is considered:

options.text: overruled by the Speaker of the Lower House

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**binding to the President**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Union Cabinet's advice to the President of India is **binding under Article 74(1) of the Indian Constitution**.
 
• The President is constitutionally obligated to act in accordance with the advice provided by the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
 
• This principle emphasizes the concept of a parliamentary democracy where the President functions as a nominal head, while real executive power resides with the Council of Ministers.
 
• The 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 made it explicit that the President "shall act in accordance with such advice."
 
• Although the President may initially return advice for reconsideration, if the same advice is sent back, the President is bound to accept it.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 74(1):** This article states that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, and the President shall act in accordance with such advice.
 
• **42nd Amendment Act (1976):** This amendment explicitly made the President's compliance with the advice of the Council of Ministers mandatory, strengthening the parliamentary system of governance.
 
• **Reconsideration Power:** While the President can send a recommendation back to the Council of Ministers for reconsideration, once the advice is reiterated, it becomes binding.
 
• **Nominal vs. Real Executive:** The President is the nominal executive head, while the Council of Ministers, led by the Prime Minister, exercises real executive authority.
 
• **Parliamentary Democracy:** India follows a parliamentary system of governance where the President acts as the constitutional head, and the Council of Ministers is responsible to the Parliament.

questions.question: Which of the following options best describes the principle of 'collective executive responsibility' as applicable to the Council of Ministers in India?

options.text: All ministers share full responsibility for government decisions.
Ministers can opt out of collective responsibility if they disagree publicly.
Only the Prime Minister is responsible for decision‑making.
Each minister is independent and is solely accountable for his/her actions.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**All ministers share full responsibility for government decisions.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Collective executive responsibility** is a principle enshrined in Article 75(3) of the Indian Constitution, which states that the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (House of the People).
 
• This principle ensures that all members of the Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, act as a single entity and take joint responsibility for the actions and policies of the government.
 
• If a decision is taken by the government, all ministers are expected to defend it publicly, even if they personally disagree with it.
 
• If a minister disagrees with a decision and is unwilling to defend it, the convention is that they must resign from their position.
 
• The principle of collective responsibility strengthens the unity of the executive and maintains the stability of the government by ensuring accountability to the legislature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 75(3):** This article specifies that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, ensuring that they act as a unified body in matters of governance.
 
• **Individual Responsibility:** While collective responsibility exists, each minister is also individually responsible for their respective departmental actions and policies.
 
• **No-Confidence Motion:** If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers, the entire Council, including the Prime Minister, is required to resign, demonstrating collective accountability.
 
• **Parliamentary Democracy:** The principle of collective responsibility is a cornerstone of parliamentary democracy, ensuring that the executive remains accountable to the legislature.
 
• **Westminster Model:** India’s collective responsibility principle is inspired by the Westminster model of governance, which emphasizes the unity and accountability of the executive branch.
